paragraphs.text: This oolong comes from [Beipu](beipu:where-it-is), a township in the south-west of Hsinchu County. It sits in low hill country between the central mountains and the coastal plain, well below the high-mountain gardens. Tea in the county is largely a [Hakka](hsinchu:hakka) trade: local families grow the leaf, make it and sell it, and many farms have passed from one generation to the next. Beipu's name is tied to [Oriental Beauty](beipu:known-for), but on a label the name says where a tea was grown. It does not say which style the tea is.

The leaf was made in 1977. At forty-nine years it belongs to Taiwan's tradition of [lao cha, old tea](taiwan-oolong:ageing). In that tradition, oolong is kept cool, dry, dark and sealed for years. From time to time it is roasted again at low heat to drive out the moisture it takes in. No standard says when an oolong becomes old. Those who give a figure put it somewhere between ten and thirty years, and this tea is well past both.

brewing.text: Ball-rolled Taiwan oolong takes hot water, about 90 to 100°C, a fairly generous amount of leaf and short steeps; the balls open slowly and give many infusions. Roasted Dong Ding takes water from about 95°C to a full boil. Aged oolong takes very hot water, in a pot that holds its heat, clay above all. Oriental Beauty is the exception and takes cooler water, about 80 to 95°C.

notice.text: A smooth, mellow, thick cup with little astringency, often plum or prune, sometimes something like medicinal herbs or ginseng, and an amber to red-brown liquor.
